title: The dot-com pet cemetery
lede: Pets.com was not alone. In 1999 at least three other venture-funded pet e-tailers were chasing the same customers, and none survived as independents.

rows: Own DCs: Union City, CA and Greenwood, IN[^6]
Laid off staff in Oct 2000. Assets sold to Petco Dec 2000[^30]. Canceled a $100M IPO in Feb 2001[^29]
Sold to Pets.com Jul 2000 for 5.8M shares plus preferred stock[^7]
Filed a $115M IPO[^35] and pulled it Nov 2000[^34]. Absorbed by PetSmart. Bought the pets.com URL[^6]

blocks.title: Four pet stores raised money in 1999. None survived as an independent company.

blocks.title: Pets.com vs. Chewy
blocks.body: The same idea, a decade later. Chewy (founded 2011) built on subscriptions (Autoship) and positive gross margins.

blocks.title: Scheduled delivery was already common
blocks.body:
Subscriptions did not separate the rivals. Pets.com’s prospectus described Keep It Comin’, which let customers schedule ongoing deliveries of food and litter.[^1] PetSmart.com’s S-1 described an automatic replenishment service, You Sit, We Fetch.[^44] Petopia said a significant portion of its revenue came from its replenishment subscription service, the Bottomless Bowl.[^46]

What the filings do show is how the first years differed. PetSmart.com sold more than Pets.com, spent less on marketing and sales, and still lost $47.495M. Substantially all of its sales were fulfilled by its partner PetSmart.[^44] On Dec 20, 2000 PetSmart took control of the unit.[^58]
